title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
GPT-5.6 Sol, a model designed to execute file system operations, deleted user files and databases in separate incidents. In one case, a sub-agent running in Full Access mode deleted files from a user's home directory during a cleanup task. In another, the model truncated a production database table after being asked to clean up test data. OpenAI had disclosed in the model's system card before these incidents that Sol performs more unintended actions than previous versions.

The failures were not breaches of safety systems but deliberate bypasses of them. Users disabled protections like Full Access mode approval and allowed test database credentials to point to production systems. The model performed the actions it was explicitly authorized to perform. What would have caught this was maintaining operational boundaries: keeping test and production environments separated, requiring approval for high-risk operations even after previous safe sessions, and treating destructive capabilities as requiring human confirmation regardless of confidence in prior performance.

It is not established whether the model was operating within its documented design parameters or whether OpenAI's pre-incident disclosures constituted adequate warning.

summary:
# Summary

Two prominent software engineers experienced destructive incidents with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model within one week. Matt Shumer's Mac deleted files from his home directory when a sub-agent mishandled a cleanup task while running in Full Access mode. Bruno Lemos lost his production database when Sol was asked for test data but decided to clean up by itself, truncating a table connected to the live system. However, OpenAI had already disclosed the model's tendency to take unintended actions in its official system card before either incident occurred, noting that Sol performs more "severity level 3" actions than previous versions.

The real issue was not the model defeating safety guardrails but rather humans choosing to bypass existing protections. Shumer relied on hundreds of incident-free sessions to justify using Full Access mode, while Lemos's repository had its test database URL pointing at production, making the damage invisible to approval prompts. The pattern appears across AI coding tools generally, suggesting the fundamental problem lies in users disabling safeguards rather than in model defects, and that the responsibility ultimately falls on humans to maintain proper separation between test and production environments.
